title-group.article-title: Safety, pharmacokinetics and CNS distribution of tralesinidase alfa administered via intracerebroventricular infusion to juvenile cynomolgus monkeys

abstract.p: Mucopolysaccharidosis Type IIIB (MPS IIIB) is an ultrarare, fatal pediatric disease with no approved therapy. It is caused by mutations in the gene encoding for lysosomal enzyme alpha-N-acetylglucosaminidase (NAGLU). Tralesinidase alfa (TA) is a fusion protein comprised of recombinant NAGLU and a modified human insulin-like growth factor 2 that is being developed as an enzyme replacement therapy for MPS IIIB. Since MPS IIIB is a pediatric disease the safety/toxicity, pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of TA were evaluated in juvenile non-human primates that were administered up to 5 weekly intracerebroventricular (ICV) or single intravenous (IV) infusions of TA. TA administered by ICV slow-, ICV isovolumetric bolus- or IV-infusion was well-tolerated, and no effects were observed on clinical observations, electrocardiographic or ophthalmologic parameters, or respiratory rates. The drug-related changes observed were limited to increased cell infiltrates in the CSF and along the ICV catheter track after ICV administration. These findings were not associated with functional changes and are associated with the use of ICV catheters. The CSF PK profiles were consistent across all conditions tested and TA distributed widely in the CNS after ICV administration. Anti-drug antibodies were observed but did not appear to significantly affect the exposure to TA. Correlations between TA concentrations in plasma and brain regions in direct contact with the cisterna magna suggest glymphatic drainage may be responsible for clearance of TA from the CNS. The data support the administration of TA by isovolumetric bolus ICV infusion to pediatric patients with MPS IIIB.

list-item.p: TA was well-tolerated after single or multiple ICV administrations to juvenile NHPs.
Safety findings were limited to increased cell infiltrates in the CSF and CNS.
TA broadly distributed to deep and superficial regions of the CNS.
ADA formation appeared to have minimal or no impact on safety or exposure.
Safety profile supports ICV administration of TA to patients with MPS IIIB disease.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Sanfilippo Syndrome Type B, or Mucopolysaccharidosis Type IIIB (MPS IIIB; OMIM #252920), is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease caused by mutations in the alpha-N-acetylglucosaminidase (NAGLU; EC 3.2.1.50) gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme NAGLU that degrades the glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate (HS). In the absence of NAGLU enzymatic activity, specific fragments of HS accumulate in lysosomes in many tissues and organs, particularly the central nervous system (CNS). Consistent with this, and in contrast with other forms of mucopolysaccharidoses, MPS IIIB patients display mild somatic and skeletal phenotypes, and instead present with early developmental delays and hyperactivity. As the disease progresses, symptoms include severe behavioral disturbances such as loss of impulse control, hyperactivity, and anxiety along with continued neurodegeneration [18], [23], [21]. Death usually occurs in the second decade of life.

Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) is a common strategy for treating lysosomal storage diseases but because of the neurological manifestations of MPS IIIB disease, an effective ERT would need to distribute widely in the brain to degrade the accumulated HS from key pathological regions. Systemically administered ERTs do not generally cross the blood-brain-barrier with sufficient efficiency to reach these deep brain regions [27], [9], [11]. However, intracerebroventricular (ICV) infusions have been shown in nonclinical studies to improve distribution of protein-based therapeutics to deep brain regions [26], [1], [11] and approved ERT cerliponase alfa (recombinant human tripeptidyl-peptidase 1, Brineura) is administered via ICV infusion to treat Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis Type 2 (CLN2) disease, another lysosomal storage disorder that primarily affects the CNS.

Tralesinidase alfa (TA) is being developed as an ERT to treat MPS IIIB disease in pediatric patients. TA is a trimer of an 89 kDa fusion protein comprised of recombinant human NAGLU and a modified fragment of the insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2; [15]) joined via an amino acid linker. The modified IGF2 tag mediates the uptake of TA into cells via the IGF2 receptor [14]. Direct CNS administration of TA to MPS IIIB mice and dogs leads to widespread brain distribution, significant clearance of HS from brain tissue, and amelioration or prevention of disease-related pathology and clinical presentation [1], [7].

Since MPS IIIB is an ultrarare, neurological, pediatric disease, toxicity studies with TA were conducted in juvenile animals. A chronic toxicity study was conducted in juvenile MPS IIIB dogs to evaluate potential exaggerated pharmacology of TA [7]. In this work, we present data from three toxicity studies in juvenile non-human primates (NHPs) that were conducted to evaluate the safety, tolerability and biodistribution of TA (summarized in Table 1). The first study in NHPs (Study 1) assessed the safety profile, pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of TA after 5 weekly doses administered by a slow 4-hour ICV infusion. The tolerability of direct systemic exposures of TA was evaluated in an additional group of animals administered escalating doses of TA by IV infusion. While cerliponase alfa is administered to CLN2 patients via a 4-h ICV infusion, MPS IIIB patients have behavioral disturbances including hyperactivity that make a similar long infusion burdensome and prohibitive. To address this clinical requirement, two additional studies in NHPs were conducted to characterize the safety profile, PK and biodistribution after a single isovolumetric bolus ICV administration of TA (Study 2) and after repeat dosing of TA via 5 weekly isovolumetric ICV bolus infusions (Study 3). In addition, Study 3 assessed the safety, tolerability and PK of TA in the clinical aCSF formulation as well as two experimental formulations. Across the three studies, the high ICV dose selected (73 mg) was the maximum feasible dose based on drug concentration and dosing volume. The lower doses were selected to cover the anticipated clinical dose, which is approximately equivalent to a 30 mg dose in non-human primates.Table 1

sec.title: Tralesinidase alfa and vehicle control articles
sec.p: TA was produced in Chinese hamster ovary cells. TA was formulated in artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF; comprised of 148 mM NaCl, 3 mM KCl, 1.4 mM CaCl2•2 H2O, 0.8 mM MgCl2•6 H2O, 0.3 mM NaH2PO4,·H2O, 0.7 mM Na2HPO4•7 H2O at pH 7.0), vehicle 1 (comprised of 233 mM Trehalose dihydrate, 15 mM NaCl, 0.3 mM NaH2PO4 *H20, 0.7 mM Na2HPO4 *7H20, pH 7), or vehicle 2 (comprised of 117 mM Trehalose dihydrate, 85 mM NaCl, 0.3 mM NaH2PO4 *H20, 0.7 mM Na2HPO4 *7H20, pH 7, 0.005% Polysorbate 20 [v/v]) at a concentration of 12 mg/ml, 29.5 mg/ml, or 20.3 mg/ml. TA and formulations were provided by BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc. All TA preparations were > 93% pure and had endotoxin levels < 0.2 EU/ml, as measured by PTS-endosafe LAL assay (Charles River Laboratories, Wilmington MA).

sec.title: Animals
sec.p: Sixty-seven (67) treatment-naïve juvenile (11–14 months old) cynomolgus monkeys (Macaca fascicularis) of Chinese origin (Alpha Genesis, Inc., Yemassee, SC) were used for the studies. Animals weighed 1.33–2.00 kg prior to dosing. Animals were housed in an AAALAC-accredited facility in compliance with NIH guidelines and the Animal Welfare Act (9 CFR 3). They were kept on a 12:12 h light:dark cycle, were fed 15 primate biscuits (PMI, Richmond, IN) per day and were provided filtered municipal water ad libitum. Study protocols were approved by authorized Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees and were conducted at Northern Biomedical Research, Inc (Spring Lake, MI) in accordance with Good Laboratory Practice Regulations (IACUC approval numbers are 074–006 A, 10MAR2014 [Study 1], 074–008 A 16MAR2015 [Study 2], and 074–017 A 04MAY2017 [Study 3]).

sec.title: Surgery
sec.p: Monkeys were implanted with catheters to the lateral ventricle (ICV) for test article or vehicle administration and to the lumbar spine (IT-L) for serial CSF sampling as previously described [26]. Briefly, prior to catheter implantation, animals had MRI scans to determine coordinates for proper ICV catheter placement. Under sedation with ketamine hydrochloride (Fort Dodge Animal Health, Fort Dodge, Iowa) and isoflurane (MWI, Meridian, Idaho) anesthesia, a polyurethane catheter (SAI Infusion Technologies) was introduced through a craniotomy into the left ventricle with the aid of stereotaxic techniques. Catheters were anchored with dental acrylic (Reliance Dental Manufacturing, Company Worth, Illinois) and a subcutaneous titanium access port (MINLOVOL; Access Technologies) was attached to the catheter. For lumbar catheter placement, an incision was made over the dorsal process at L4, L5, or L6 and the polyurethane catheter (SAI Infusion Technologies) was inserted and advanced to the area of the thoraco-lumbar junction via a hemilaminectomy. A subcutaneous titanium access port (MINLOVOL; Instech Solomon) was attached to the catheter and proper placement was confirmed by the ability to sample CSF. Animals were provided a post-surgical recovery period of at least two weeks prior to dose administration.

sec.title: Study designs
sec.p:
Animals were randomly assigned to treatment groups by body weight, assigned a unique animal/study number, and identified with a tattoo and an implanted transponder. In Study 1, animals received 5 weekly doses of 8, 24, or 73 mg of TA or vehicle via a slow 4-h ICV infusion (Table 2). The highest ICV dose (73 mg) of TA was the maximal feasible dose based on drug concentration and dosing volume. Animals in Group 5 were administered a bolus IV infusion of vehicle (aCSF) followed by escalating doses of TA (Table 2). The highest IV dose (203 mg/kg) was the maximal feasible dose and was expected to provide a large margin over the anticipated peripheral exposure observed in MPS IIIB subjects. In Study 2, monkeys received a single isovolumetric ICV bolus infusion of 30 or 73 mg TA or vehicle, or a 4-h ICV infusion of 73 mg TA and were observed for 2 or 14 days before necropsy (Table 3). In Study 3, animals received 5 weekly isovolumetric ICV bolus infusions of 30 mg TA formulated in aCSF or two other exploratory formulations (see above for details). Animals in Group 1 received Vehicle 2 alone with no test article. Monkeys were observed for 2 days after the final dose prior to necropsy (Table 4). In Studies 2 and 3, the 30 mg dose level was selected because it is thought to scale to the selected clinical dose of 300 mg based on relative brain mass of juvenile monkeys (∼100 g) and pediatric humans (∼1000 g).Table 2

sec.title: Dose administration
sec.p: TA was administered ICV either by a rapid isovolumetric bolus infusion (0.5 ml/min) or by a non-isovolumetric slow infusion (0.88 ml/h) as described previously [26] using a calibrated syringe pump (New Era syringe pump [Model NE-300]). For the rapid isovolumetric bolus administration, 2.5 ml CSF was collected via cisterna magna (CM) spinal tap with the animals under anesthesia (8 mg/kg ketamine (Fort Dodge Animal Health, Fort Dodge, Iowa) with isoflurane (MWI, Meridian, Idaho) [Study 2] or 0.04 mg/kg dexmedetomidine (Orion Corp., Espoo, Finland) and 2.5 mg/kg ketamine [Study 3]). Immediately after the CSF draw, 2.5 ml TA or vehicle were administered through the ICV port/catheter system over 5 min at a rate of 0.5 ml/min followed by 0.25 ml of PBS (Life Technologies [Gibco brand], Grand Island, NY) to flush the rest of the dose from the system. For the slow infusion, 2.5 ml TA was infused at a rate of 0.88 ml/h over 4 h with no prior CSF removal. IV administration of TA was conducted over 5 min through the saphenous vein at a rate of 3 ml/min for a dose volume of 10 ml/kg. Each IV dose was flushed with 0.2 ml 0.9% sodium chloride (Hospira, Inc., Lake Forest Illinois). Each dose escalation was separated from the previous dose by 3–4 days.

sec.title: Safety endpoints
sec.p: Animals were observed at least once daily for clinical signs, and morbidity and mortality beginning after surgery and throughout the study period. Body weights were recorded prior to surgery, on the day(s) of dosing, weekly, and at necropsy. The safety pharmacology core battery (CNS, cardiovascular, and respiratory systems) was evaluated as part of the general toxicity studies to reduce animal use. Physical and neurological examinations were performed once pre-study, and prior to necropsy (Study 1 ICV groups and Study 2 [additional exams were conducted at 6 h post dose for monkeys in Study 2]), pre-study and 24 h post last dose (Study 1 IV group), or pre-study and 24 h post doses 2 and 4 (Study 3). Food consumption was monitored, and electrocardiography and ophthalmologic examinations were performed pre-study and 6 h post dose (Study 1 ICV groups), pre-study and 24 h post last dose (Study 1 IV group), or pre-study and 24 h post doses 2 and 4 (Study 3).

sec.title: Clinical pathology
sec.p: Clinical pathology parameters in blood (hematology, serum chemistry, and coagulation), urine (urinalysis), and CSF (CSF chemistry and total cell count) were evaluated (Antech GLP, Morrisville, NC). Blood was collected from 12 h fasted animals pre-study and either prior to necropsy (Study 1 and Study 2) or 4 h after doses 2 and 5 (Study 3). Additional blood samples (2–3 drops) were collected at the first ICV dose (Study 1, Groups 1–4) and at each IV dose (Study 1, Group 5) and were measured by a blood glucose monitor (Abbott Diabetes Care). Urine was collected pre-study and prior to necropsy for urinalysis. CSF samples were collected from fasted ICV-administered animals from the lumbar catheter or via CM tap prior to each dose and at necropsy (Studies 2 and 3). CSF samples were collected from fasted ICV-administered animals in Study 1 prior to dosing, prior to and 24 h post Doses 2, 3 and 4, and prior to necropsy. Additional CSF samples were collected halfway through Dose 4 and 2 h post Dose 4 (Study 1). Partial catheter obstruction in some animals prevented CSF sampling at some time points.

sec.title: PK and antibody analysis
sec.p: TA concentrations in plasma and CSF after ICV or IV administration were evaluated to assess the disposition of TA between these two compartments and characterize differences between the two infusion rates. Blood and CSF were collected from ICV-administered animals prior to dosing, immediately after infusion (∼2 min post infusion) and 0.5, 2, 6, 10, 24, 48, 72, 96, 120, 168, and 336 (prior to necropsy) h post dose (not all time points are relevant for all groups of animals due to scheduled necropsy times; samples from Study 3 were collected only at Doses 1 and 4). In addition, monkeys that received the ICV slow infusion of TA (Study 1 and Study 2, Group 4) had blood and CSF samples collected halfway through the infusion (∼2 h after start of infusion). Partial catheter obstruction in some animals prevented CSF sampling at some time points. Blood samples were collected from IV-administered animals prior to each dose administration and 0.25, 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, and 48 h post each dose of TA and at necropsy (Study 1, Group 5). TA concentrations were measured in CSF samples collected at the above time points from IV-administered animals (Study 1, Group 5) and the data have been published [11]. Plasma was separated out in potassium EDTA tubes (VWR Scientific Products, West Chester, PA) at ∼2400 rpm at ∼4ᵒC. Due to a lack of stability of TA at low concentrations in plasma and CSF, only the samples around the anticipated Cmax (immediately post infusion and 0.5 and 2 h post infusion for plasma and immediately after infusion and 0.5 h post infusion for CSF) were analyzed from Studies 1 and 2. In Study 3, plasma and CSF were collected in tubes containing 1% Tween-20 (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO) for a final concentration of 0.05% Tween-20 to improve the stability of TA in the samples and allowed for analysis of all time points collected. TA concentrations in plasma and CSF were measured as described [11], [7]. The lower limit of quantitation (LLOQ) was 0.823 ng/ml for the plasma and CSF assays. Total anti-TA antibodies were analyzed in serum and CSF samples collected pre-study for Studies 1 and 3; prior to ICV Doses 3, and 5 and at necropsy (Study 1, Groups 1–4); at necropsy (Study 1, Group 5); or prior to Dose 4 (Study 3). Total anti-TA antibodies were measured using an electrochemiluminescent immunoassay technology platform (ICON Laboratory Services, Whitesboro, NY). Samples harvested for test article analysis (plasma and CSF) and antibody analysis (serum and CSF) were placed into Nunc® 377267 Thermo Scientific CryoTube™ vials.

sec.title: Necropsy and tissue collection
sec.p: Animals were euthanized at time points indicated in Table 2, Table 3, Table 4. They were sedated with ketamine HCl (8 mg/kg, intramuscular injection, Zoetis, New York, NY), maintained on an isoflurane (MWI, Meridian, Idaho)/oxygen mixture, and provided with an intravenous bolus of heparin Na (200 IU/kg, Sagent Pharmaceuticals, Schaumburg, IL). Animals were perfused via the left cardiac ventricle with 0.001% sodium nitrite (Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals, Inc., Hazelwood, MO) in chilled 0.9% saline (VWR Scientific Products, West Chester, PA). Peripheral organs including heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, stomach, ovaries, uterus, vagina, testes, urethra, seminal vesicles, and prostate were collected from all animals and saved in 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF, VWR Scientific Products, West Chester, PA; Study 1). Brain, dorsal nerve roots and ganglion, gross lesions, sciatic nerve (proximal and distal), spinal cord (cervical, thoracic, and lumbar), sural nerve, tibial nerve, and trigeminal ganglion were collected for in-depth analysis (Studies 1, 2 and 3). Brains were cut in a brain matrix at 3 mm coronal slice thickness. The first slice and every other slice thereafter were fixed in 10% NBF (VWR Scientific Products, West Chester, PA) for histopathology. The second slice and every other slice thereafter were frozen for biodistribution. Before freezing, two 4 mm round specimens (one from a superficial [<3 mm deep, with respect to the ventricle] and one from a deep [> 3 mm deep, with respect to the ventricle] area) of cerebral (frontal) cortex, occipital cortex, cerebellum, striatum, medulla, midbrain, and thalamus were weighed and snap frozen for TA biodistribution analysis. An approximately 1 cm section of spinal cord from the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar regions were collected, weighed, and snap frozen for biodistribution analysis. The remainder of the spinal cord was saved in 10% NBF for histopathology.

sec.title: Tissue NAGLU analysis
sec.p: NAGLU levels (TA that has been taken up into the lysosome and had the IGF2 tag cleaved off) in brain regions and spinal cord were measured temporally post ICV infusion in Study 1 to provide an approximate tissue half-life and estimate an appropriate frequency of dosing in MPS IIIB patients. In Study 3, NAGLU levels in brain regions and spinal cord were measured 48 h after the last dose. NAGLU levels were measured in tissue homogenates by ELISA as described [11], [7]. The assay detects both human and monkey forms of NAGLU and has an LLOQ of 0.492 ng/ml. Mean NAGLU concentrations in each region were normalized to the concentrations in the control groups and results are expressed as fold over endogenous monkey NAGLU levels.

sec.title: Histopathology
sec.p: All histopathological analyses were conducted by ToxPath Specialists (now StageBio). Analyses were conducted on heart, kidney, liver, lung and gross peripheral lesions from animals administered TA by ICV infusion (Study 1). All peripheral tissues collected were evaluated from animals administered TA by IV infusion (Study 1). An extensive histopathological analysis was conducted of the brain, spinal cord, dorsal and ventral spinal nerve roots and ganglia, and sciatic, tibial, and sural nerves (Studies 1–3). Brain sections were embedded in paraffin and sectioned at approximately 5 µm. Sections were stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E), Fluoro-Jade B (to identify neuronal necrosis), ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule (an immunohistochemical indicator of activated microglia; Wako 019–19741, 1:600 and 1:1200 dilutions), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (an immunohistochemical indicator for astrocytosis; Dako Z0334, 1:800 dilution). The spinal cord, dorsal spinal nerve routes, ganglion and ventral nerve roots, and peripheral nerves were embedded in paraffin, sectioned using a five-micron block advance and stained with H&E and Bielschowsky’s silver (control and high dose animals only) to visualize axons, dendrites, and neural filaments. Additionally, a transverse section of the tibial nerve was osmicated, embedded in resin, sectioned at approximately 1 µm, and stained with Toluidine Blue to visualize myelin and cellular details. Any gross CNS lesions detected at necropsy were embedded in paraffin and stained with H&E.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Body weights, body weight changes, food consumption, respiratory rate, body temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, CSF cell count, and clinical pathology parameters were analyzed by a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and comparison of the control group (Group 1) to Groups 2 – 4 (Study 1) or Groups 1 and 3 (Study 3) by Dunnett’s test when n ≥ 3. Statistical analyses were not performed on data from the animals in Group 5 (Study 1), Group 4 (Study 2) or in Study 3 due to small number of animals or the absence of concurrent controls. All other statistical analyses were conducted as indicated.

sec.title: Clinical observations and safety pharmacology endpoints
sec.p: ICV administration of up to 5 weekly doses of TA given via 4-h infusion (0.88 ml/h) or isovolumetric bolus infusion (0.5 ml/min) were well-tolerated up to 73 mg/dose regardless of the formulation. Single IV administration up to 203 mg/kg was also well-tolerated. There were no TA- or vehicle-related changes in clinical observations, body weight, food consumption, or physical and neurological examinations across the studies. No TA- or vehicle-related effects on respiratory rates, or ophthalmologic or electrocardiographic parameters were observed in any animals.

sec.title: Clinical pathology
sec.p: No changes in hematology, serum chemistry, coagulation, or urinalysis parameters were observed in any of the dosing groups from any of the studies. Mild increases in WBC in the CSF were noted in all ICV-administered dosing groups across the three studies. While increased WBC in CSF was observed in monkeys administered vehicle, cell counts increased with increasing dose of TA. These changes were observed in the CSF within 24 h post ICV administration. In all cases, the increased WBC was comprised of increased eosinophils and monocytes. There were no significant TA- or vehicle-related changes in CSF chemistry parameters in any of the dose groups. CSF was not analyzed for cellularity or chemistry changes in the IV-treated animals.

Hypoglycemia or hypoglycorrhachia could be a potential clinical consequence of the interaction of the IGF2 tag of TA with either the IGF2 receptor or the insulin receptor in blood or CSF, respectively. Glucose levels were measured in serum and CSF over the course of the three studies. No TA-related changes in serum or CSF glucose were observed in any dose group. Administration of TA via IV infusion also did not produce discernable changes in serum glucose levels.

sec.title: TA PK and antibody response in CSF and plasma
sec.p:
Typical CSF and plasma PK analyses were not possible from the data collected from Studies 1 and 2 due to sample instability of lower concentrations of TA after a single freeze thaw. For these studies, it was only possible to measure TA levels around the anticipated Cmax; consequently, only trend observations could be made. The mean concentrations of TA in plasma for males and females were generally below the stability cutoff following ICV infusion so no further analysis was conducted. TA exposure (Cmax) tended to increase with dose in CSF following ICV infusion (Supplementary Table 1) and in plasma following IV injection (Table S2). The Cmax values in CSF after a 4-h infusion were 626,000 ng/ml for the 8 mg dose, 2240,000 ng/ml for the 24 mg dose and 5250,000 ng/ml for the 73 mg dose from Study 1 (Day 29) and 6310,000 ng/ml from Study 2. Similarly, the Cmax values in CSF after an isovolumetric bolus administration were 6440,000 ng/ml for the 30 mg dose and 13,900,000 ng/ml for the 73 mg dose (Study 2, Day 1). The mean TA Cmax values for males and females tended to be dose proportional in CSF following ICV infusion and in plasma following IV injection. Sex differences were generally less than 2-fold in TA Cmax values following ICV infusion or IV injection. The presence of anti-drug antibodies (ADA) in CSF and plasma was assessed in ICV-administered animals from Study 1; Study 2 involved a single dose of TA so ADA was not expected to play a role in the timeframe evaluated. None of the monkeys tested positive for ADA in serum or CSF prior to dosing and none of the vehicle-treated animals tested positive for ADA at any time during the study. The presence of ADA in CSF was confirmed in 16 of 19 animals administered TA and was confirmed in serum of all animals administered TA (Table 5). Due to the limited PK dataset, it was not possible to evaluate the impact of ADA on TA exposure.Table 5

PK and ADA analyses were possible from the data collected from Study 3 after it was discovered that the addition of 0.05% Tween-20 stabilized TA in CSF and plasma. Exposures in plasma and CSF after Dose 1 and Dose 4 were comparable (Fig. 1, Table 5). Exposure to TA in plasma was approximately 0.2–1% of the exposure in CSF for all formulations, but plasma exposure varied widely with AUC0−t ranging from 49,100 to 436,000 ng-h/ml among animals and doses. No accumulation of TA was observed in plasma or CSF after multiple weekly doses of TA, consistent with the drug half-life in CSF of less than 4 h. No statistically significant differences in exposure to TA formulated in aCSF or the two experimental formulations tested in Study 3 (Vehicle 1 and Vehicle 2). None of the monkeys had measurable levels of ADA in CSF or plasma prior to dosing, and none of the monkeys administered vehicle had measurable levels of ADA at any time during the study. The presence of ADA in CSF was confirmed in only three of twelve animals administered TA and was confirmed in serum of all animals administered TA (Table 6). The exposure of TA in CSF and plasma was generally similar between Dose 1 and Dose 4 regardless of the presence of ADA. The ratio of the CSF AUC0−t at Dose 4 compared to Dose 1 ranged from 79% to 112%. Despite significant inter-animal variability in plasma PK, the plasma AUC0−t at Dose 4 compared to Dose 1 ranged from 32% to 80% (Supplementary Table 3).Fig. 1

Taken together these data suggest that exposure in CSF was generally similar between studies and/or formulations and ADAs had minimal impact on TA exposure.

sec.title: TA biodistribution in the CNS
sec.p:
TA levels were detected throughout the brain and spinal cord in monkeys from Studies 1 and 3 following ICV administration (Fig. 2, Supplementary Figure 1). Exposure to TA in brain and spinal cord increased with dose from 8 to 24–73 mg (Fig. 2). The levels of TA detected in across brain regions were generally similar between Studies 1 and 3 suggesting that infusion rate did not affect the biodistribution. The half-life (t1/2) of TA in brain tissue was calculated where possible from male and female monkeys from Group 4 (73 mg) in Study 1. Values ranged from 105 to 210 h (4–9 days; Table 7). The t1/2 values were generally similar in deep and superficial tissue.Fig. 2

sec.title: Correlation of TA levels in plasma and CNS tissue
sec.p:
Given the direct administration of TA into the CNS compartment, concentrations observed in plasma must be due to exchange between the brain parenchyma and the plasma. TA concentrations were variable throughout the brain regions tested (Figs. 2 and S1), and we hypothesized that there could be a correlation between concentrations in regions of the brain proximal to the sites of CSF flow and the peripheral compartment where TA eventually drains. Indeed, a correlation was observed between the circulating concentration of TA in plasma (AUC) and levels in the cerebellum obtained from samples from monkeys in Study 3 (Pearson’s correlation r = 0.81, p = 0.001) and medulla oblongata (Pearson’s correlation r = 0.68, p < 0.02, Fig. 3), which are two regions that are in direct contact with the cisterna magna through which CSF flows on its way out of the CNS into the periphery. No correlation was observed between plasma exposure and TA levels in other brain regions, such as thalamus, cortex or brainstem.Fig. 3
: Correlation between exposure of TA in plasma (AUC) and brain regions in direct contact with the cisterna magna; superficial cerebellum (A) and medulla oblongata (B). Each data point is a single monkey.Fig. 3

sec.title: Necropsy
sec.p: Gross lesions were present at similar frequencies in all dosing groups at necropsy, including the vehicle-control group, and none were attributed to TA administration. Gross lesions in the CNS were observed along the ICV catheter track in several animals across all studies and dosing groups. These were attributed to complications of the ICV catheter placement and/or dosing procedures and/or the presence of the foreign indwelling catheter. There were no TA- or vehicle-related changes in organ weights for any dosing group in any study.

sec.title: Histopathology
sec.p:
Increased cellular infiltrates (mononuclear cells and eosinophils) in the meninges (brain and spinal cord), adjacent to the ICV catheter track, and adjacent to the lateral ventricle were observed across all studies in all monkeys outfitted with an ICV catheter. While the infiltrates were observed in the ICV vehicle-treated animals, they were more pronounced in monkeys administered TA by ICV infusion. These changes were most consistent in the monkeys administered 73 mg of TA, i.e., the highest dose tested, by either slow infusion or isovolumetric bolus infusion (Study 1 and Study 2) but some increase in infiltrates were also observed at the 30 mg dose level (isovolumetric bolus infusion, Study 3). The increase in infiltrates was consistent across the three formulations tested in Study 3. In Study 1, increased perivascular infiltrates were also observed in the ipsilateral and contralateral hemisphere in monkeys administered TA via ICV infusion as compared to the vehicle control monkeys. A representative image of the increased infiltrates observed in the 73 mg dose group from Study 1 is presented in Fig. 4.Fig. 4
Representative histopathology images from high dose monkey from Study 1. (A) Cellular infiltrates observed along the catheter track. (B) Cellular infiltrates observed in the lateral ventricle (LV). These images were taken from two different monkeys in the 73 mg dose group.Fig. 4

All other microscopic changes observed in animals administered TA or vehicle by ICV infusion were attributed to the presence of ICV or IT-L catheters or complications during dosing procedures. An increase in gliosis/microgliosis, astrocytosis, neuronal cell loss, fibrosis, clotted blood, and inflammation occurred along the catheter track. These changes occurred across all dose groups in all studies: in monkeys administered TA or vehicle via slow ICV infusion or isovolumetric bolus ICV infusion, received a single dose or 5 weekly doses, or were administered TA in aCSF or two other experimental formulations. Two animals from Study 3 had areas of necrosis in or adjacent to the white matter/corona radiata, which were associated cellular infiltrates and glial reactions. This necrosis was most likely due to complications during the dosing procedures and not directly associated with the presence of TA or the formulation. No microscopic changes related to TA were observed in peripheral tissues of monkeys dosed by ICV infusion.

An in-depth histopathological analysis was conducted on peripheral tissues, including reproductive tissues, from monkeys administered TA by IV infusion (Study 1). There were no microscopic changes in any of the peripheral tissues analyzed that were attributable to TA even at the highest dose of 203 mg/kg. Additional analysis of nervous system tissues in these animals found no changes that were related to TA.

sec.title: Safety of TA
sec.p: TA administered weekly up to 5 weeks via ICV infusion did not produce safety signals of concern in cynomolgus monkeys, whether TA was administered via a slow infusion (over 4 h) or as a fast isovolumetric bolus or whether TA was administered in aCSF or two other experimental formulations. Juvenile monkeys between 11- and 14-months of age were used, which is a relevant age window [4], [12] since pediatric patients have been included in clinical trials with TA [17] There were no changes in clinical signs, ECG, neurological parameters, respiratory rates, or clinical chemistry parameters. Increased cellularity was observed in the CSF of all ICV-implanted animals in the three studies, which correlated to the increase in cellular infiltrates found in the meninges of all animals outfitted with an ICV catheter. While these findings were observed in all monkeys including the vehicle control animals, the increase in cell count was more apparent in monkeys administered TA, in particular the animals administered 73 mg TA. The findings related to the ICV catheters or dosing procedures were expected consequences of the use of these devices in nonclinical species [5], [26], [7] and the potential test article-related changes are not specific to the administration of TA. These are typical findings associated with the introduction of a protein-based test article into the CSF [5], [26]. Additionally, pleocytosis, specifically eosinophilic granulocytosis, has been observed in humans after ICV administration [16], [10]. The increased infiltrates were not associated with histological changes and did not result in functional changes in any of the three studies. Therefore, they were not considered adverse and are not suggestive of a potential safety concern.

The lack of safety signals after administration of TA is similar to what has been observed with other ERTs including cerliponase alfa, which is also administered via ICV infusion [22], [13], [3], [8], [24], [25], [2], [26]. Like cerliponase alfa, TA is inactive until it is taken up into the acidic environment of the lysosome where it cleaves its specific substrate HS. Exaggerated pharmacology and off-target toxicity are unlikely due to the specific activity and efficient lysosomal uptake of TA. Hypoglycorrhachia or hypoglycemia are potential consequences of the modified IGF2 tag on TA. Similar to what has been reported in dogs [7] and humans [17], no changes in glucose levels in CSF were observed after ICV administration of TA to cynomolgus monkeys.

In line with the lack of TA-related effects in the CNS, no changes were observed in the periphery after ICV or IV administration of TA. While ICV administration is not likely to result in high peripheral exposures, increasing IV administration of TA up to 203 mg/kg is anticipated to result in systemic exposures much higher than the expected peripheral exposure in the clinic after ICV administration. No changes in glucose levels in plasma were observed after ICV or IV administration of TA suggesting that the modified IGF2 tag does not interfere with glucose signaling. In line with what was observed in MPS IIIB dogs [7], no microscopic changes in peripheral tissues, including reproductive tissues, were observed even in monkeys administered TA by IV infusion even at exaggerated systemic exposure levels.

sec.title: CSF and plasma PK and CNS distribution
sec.p: Patients with MPS IIIB have accumulation of HS in the CNS and visceral organs and present with primarily neurological symptoms. Thus, any viable therapy must address the disease pathology in the CNS. TA administered via conventional intravenous administration does not cross the blood brain barrier to appreciable levels [11]. Similar to what has been observed after a single bolus ICV administration to monkeys [11] or chronic CNS administration to dogs [7], weekly ICV administration of TA to monkeys either by slow infusion or by isovolumetric bolus infusion resulted in widespread distribution to superficial and deep brain regions relative to the ventricle. The t1/2 in CNS tissue was between 4 and 9 days, which supports weekly or every-other-week dosing of TA in the clinic.

ADA were detected in serum and CSF of monkeys in Study 1 and 3 and there was no impact of ADA on safety in either study. Due to PK sample instability in Study 1, it was only possible to assess the effect of ADA on TA exposure in Study 3; ADAs were not expected to play a role in Study 2 since it was a single dose study. Despite the presence of anti-TA antibodies in the CSF of three monkeys and in the serum of all monkeys by Dose 4, the exposure of TA in CSF and serum was generally similar between Dose 1 and Dose 4 suggesting that ADA had little effect on TA exposure. ADA were detected in CSF and serum of MPS IIIB subjects administered up to 300 mg TA by isovolumetric ICV bolus [17] and MPS IIIB dogs treated with up to 48 mg TA by direct CNS infusion [7], [17]. Despite the presence of ADA, TA reduced HS levels in CSF and CNS tissue, reduced hepatomegaly and improved cognitive function after 20 months of treatment in MPS IIIB dogs illustrating that ADA had no apparent neutralizing effect [7]. Similarly, TA treatment normalized HS levels in the CSF of MPS IIIB subjects and the reduction was sustained over the 48-week study [17].

sec.title: Plasma PK and correlation between plasma exposure and CNS distribution
sec.p: Solutes, e.g., HS and drug, circulate from the CSF through the subarachnoid space to be drained out of the brain parenchyma either via the meningeal lymphatic vessels and the deep cervical lymph nodes or via the arachnoid villi into the blood stream [20], [19]. After ICV administration, low levels of TA reached the systemic circulation (0.2–1% of that in the CSF), as measured in monkeys from Study 3. Similar findings were observed in MPS IIIB dogs administered TA by ICV infusion [7] and in monkeys administered cerliponase alfa by ICV infusion [26].

To reach peripheral circulation from the CSF, TA must go through the cisterna magna, which is part of the subarachnoid space. The cerebellum and medulla oblongata are in direct contact with the cisterna magna and this proximity could explain the preferential correlation between TA plasma concentration and TA quantification in cerebellum and medulla. For TA to reach the periphery from the CNS, the CSF drainage system must be functional. Recent literature has suggested that functionality of the meningeal lymphatics plays a crucial role in the efficacy of immunotherapies targeting Aβ amyloid in Alzheimer’s patients [6]. By analogy, it could be possible that MPS IIIB subjects might not be able to fully benefit from TA therapy and eliminate HS from their brain parenchyma unless they have a functioning glymphatic draining system. This could explain why it takes some subjects longer to benefit from TA [17]. The correlation between plasma drug concentration and exposure in key brain regions could be relevant for understanding normalization of HS in CNS tissue and important for predicting early beneficial effects on cognition.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: We have demonstrated the safety, tolerability and favorable PK and CNS distribution of TA after single or multiple ICV administrations via a slow or fast infusion to juvenile non-human primates. TA was well-tolerated whether formulated in aCSF or in two experimental formulations. The safety findings were limited to increased cell infiltrates in the CSF and CNS, which are frequently observed with ICV catheters and other ERTs administered via ICV infusion. No changes in safety pharmacology endpoints and no systemic or off-target effects (including in reproductive tissues) were observed, even with exaggerated systemic exposure via direct IV dosing. Widespread distribution to deep and superficial CNS regions was observed across the three monkey studies and the CNS tissue half-life was between 4 and 9 days supporting weekly or every-other-week dosing in the clinic. ADA formation appeared to have minimal or no impact on exposure. The correlation between CNS biodistribution and exposure in the plasma suggests that TA administered via ICV infusion filters into the periphery via glymphatic drainage. The data presented here are in line with what has been observed in dogs administered up to 48 mg TA every two weeks for up to 20 months by direct CNS infusion and the safety profile is similar to what has been observed in MPS IIIB patients administered 300 mg TA every week. The juvenile toxicity studies conducted with TA support the current clinical program and dosing of TA via isovolumetric bolus ICV infusion to pediatric patients with MPS IIIB disease.
